tur38-22: Pain due to a serious disease
tur38-23: Causes such as a fracture, infection, tumour or cauda equina syndrome are found in fewer than 1% of people with low back pain. That is why warning signs matter.
tur38-25: Mechanical or inflammatory? Low back pain that starts slowly in young people and lasts for months is sometimes caused by an inflammatory disease of the spine (axial spondyloarthritis, for example ankylosing spondylitis). According to the international ASAS criteria, in back pain lasting more than 3 months, inflammatory back pain is suspected if at least four of these five features are present: onset before age 40, an insidious and slow onset, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, and pain at night that eases on getting up. This is not a diagnosis and the criteria are not perfect; if you have these features, see a doctor. Ankylosing spondylitis guide →

tur38-32: Most episodes of low back pain get better.Low back pain does not inevitably get worse with age.
tur38-33: Thoughts and behaviours matter.Negative thoughts, avoiding movement, negative expectations of recovery and difficulty coping with pain are more strongly linked to long-lasting pain than tissue damage is.
tur38-34: Scans do not determine how the pain will go.An MRI or X-ray does not show how the current pain will progress.
tur38-35: Movement is safe.Gradual exercise and movement in all directions are safe and healthy for the spine.
tur38-36: Posture matters less than people think.In research, spinal posture while sitting, standing and lifting was not linked to low back pain starting or continuing (these studies are mostly observational).
tur38-37: Weak core muscles do not cause low back pain.Keeping your trunk muscles strong is good; but some people with low back pain over-tense these muscles, so being able to relax them when they are not needed also matters.
tur38-38: Gradual loading strengthens the spine.Moving and loading the spine in gradually increasing amounts is safe and makes it more resilient.
tur38-39: Flare-ups do not mean damage.Pain flare-ups are linked more to changes in activity, stress and mood than to structural damage.
tur38-40: Effective care is relatively cheap and safe.It includes personalised information, support to build a positive outlook, and guidance on physical and social activity, sleep, a healthy weight and staying at work.
tur38-41: A short history of low back pain treatment
tur38-42: For a long time, bed rest was a commonly recommended treatment for low back pain. Research over the last 40 years has shown that staying active, exercise for long-lasting pain and understanding pain correctly are more helpful.
tur38-43: In a study of 203 people with acute low back pain, those advised 2 days of bed rest did as well as those advised 7 days, and lost 45% fewer work days.
tur38-44: In a study of 186 employees with acute low back pain in Finland, those who continued their usual activities as far as pain allowed recovered faster than those who had bed rest and those who did back-mobilising exercises taught by a physiotherapist.
tur38-45: In a study of 380 patients in the USA, those who had a rapid MRI instead of an X-ray as their first imaging test were in almost the same condition a year later as those who had an X-ray.
tur38-46: A review of MRI and CT scans of people without pain showed that disc wear and bulging become very common with age.
tur38-47: The UK NICE guideline was published: for low back pain it advised against routine imaging, corsets, traction, acupuncture, TENS and spinal injection treatments; staying active came to the fore.
tur38-48: The American College of Physicians (ACP) recommended non-drug treatments before medicines: heat, massage, acupuncture or manipulation for pain lasting under 12 weeks; options such as exercise, yoga, tai chi and cognitive behavioural therapy for long-lasting pain.
tur38-49: A series of articles in The Lancet addressed low back pain as a global public health problem and stressed that fewer than 1% of people with low back pain have a serious disease.
tur38-50: A review of 95 studies showed that new low back pain mostly eases considerably in the first 6 weeks, while improvement in long-lasting pain is slow.
tur38-51: NICE withdrew its recommendations on psychological treatments from the guideline because part of the evidence they relied on was later retracted, and did not replace them; the American College of Physicians' 2017 guideline, however, includes cognitive behavioural therapy among the options.
tur38-52: It is the foundation of treatment for long-lasting low back pain: people who exercised had on average 15 points less pain out of 100 at 3 months than those receiving no treatment, usual care or placebo. The best exercise is the one you can do regularly. For new pain, the most important thing is to stay active and carry on with daily activities.
tur38-53: In the NICE guideline, mobilisation, manipulation and soft tissue techniques can be considered only as part of a package that includes exercise, not on their own; in the ACP guideline, manipulation on its own is also among the options, but its effect is small.

tur38-81: Is my back hurting because of bad posture?
tur38-82: In research, posture while sitting, standing and lifting was not linked to low back pain starting or continuing (these studies are mostly observational). If staying in the same position for a long time makes your pain worse, change position often and get up and walk from time to time.

tur38-96: How serious is it? Four grades
tur38-97: An international expert group (the Bone and Joint Decade Task Force, 2008) divided neck pain into four grades by severity. Most neck pain is in the first two grades.

tur38-103: No signs of a serious cause. Pain control and getting active early are recommended to prevent long-term limitation.

tur38-111: Neck straightening, MRI findings and "bad posture"
tur38-112: Seeing "loss of the neck curve" on an X-ray report worries many people. In a study comparing 107 people, 54 with neck pain and 53 without, there was no difference between the two groups in neck curvature. According to the researchers, such findings in people with neck pain should be considered coincidental; that is, they may not indicate the cause of the pain.
tur38-113: The same applies to "disc bulging" on MRI reports: in a study examining the neck MRIs of 1,211 people without pain, disc bulging was seen in 87.6%; even in their 20s it was present in 73% of men and 78% of women.
tur38-114: There is a similar finding for posture while texting: in a cross-sectional study of 150 young people aged 18–21 in Brazil, no link was found between neck posture while texting and neck pain. The study is small and did not look at the effect of a bent posture over many years. If staying in the same position for a long time is uncomfortable, change position often.
tur38-115: A short history of neck pain research
tur38-116: Research over the last 20 years has highlighted the importance of exercise, staying active and treatment matched to the type of pain.
tur38-117: The Bone and Joint Decade Task Force took a fresh look at neck pain: it divided pain into four grades by severity and reported that the pain does not completely resolve in at least half of cases, and that recovery appears to be affected more by psychological factors and work stress than by physical factors. In research, 50–85% of people with neck pain reported neck pain again 1–5 years later.

tur38-153: Can bending over my phone damage my neck?
tur38-154: There is no evidence that bending the neck to look at a phone damages the neck; but there are few studies on this. In a study of 150 young people aged 18–21 in Brazil, no link was found between neck posture while texting and neck pain. The study is small and cross-sectional; the effect of a bent posture over many years was not examined. If staying in the same position for a long time is uncomfortable, take breaks and change position.
